UX Case Study · Inova Health System · 2025

Inova Assist, an AI that
did the work, not just chat.

ChatGPT was blocked for data safety, but staff still needed it, so they kept using it on their phones. Rebuilding a safe chat wouldn't have won them back. I designed an assistant that could act inside the tools staff already used, open and manage ServiceNow tickets, work on their files, summarize and set up meetings, with ChatGPT's chat and the hospital's safety underneath. That is what made people switch.

The short version

The whole case, in three lines.

The problem

ChatGPT got blocked, but the need didn't. Staff kept using it on their phones.

What I did

Designed a safe assistant that did things ChatGPT can't, inside the tools staff already used, and owned what shipped first.

The result

91% finished their task. 8 of 8 said they'd switch from their workaround.

"The tool was useful. The problem was that patient data was leaving the building with it."
Why the project started

The problem

Blocking the tool didn't stop the risk.
It just hid it.

IT blocked ChatGPT, but staff were already leaning on it to get real work done. The ban didn't remove the risk, it removed the hospital's view of it. And a safe chat box on its own wouldn't win anyone back, because the workaround was useful. The replacement had to do more than talk.

What the ban actually did
  • The work didn't go away. Staff kept using ChatGPT on personal devices. The need was real, so the workaround stayed
  • Now with zero oversight. Patient-adjacent data still went out, just off hospital systems entirely
  • No safe alternative existed. People needed to summarize notes, raise tickets, work on files, and had nothing sanctioned that could
  • A mandate can't beat convenience. If the official tool was just a slower chat, they'd quietly go right back
What would make people switch
  • Do the work, not just answer. Act inside the tools they already used, tickets, files, meetings, so it saved real steps
  • At least as capable as ChatGPT. Same engine, no sense of a downgrade, or no one moves
  • Safe by where it runs. Inside the hospital's own protected systems, so data never left
  • Allowed, and easy. Sanctioned, already signed in, and calm to use, not a compliance maze
Compliance was the floor, not the goal. Keeping data inside the hospital's systems was the boundary the product had to sit within, and engineering owned most of it. My problem was everything above that line: making the safe tool more useful than the risky one.

What I learned

Listening before building.

Before designing anything, I ran interviews and workshops with clinicians, analysts, IT, and compliance. The goal was a focused MVP, not a feature list.

The vision

"A secure enterprise AI assistant that helps employees find information, analyze documents, and finish tasks, inside the workflows they already use."

The setup

Who we talked to, and what was at stake.

Users

Clinicians, analysts, IT and corporate staff

Primary and secondary users across the organization.

Pain points

Fragmented workflows, scattered tools

Slow access to information forces constant context switching.

Business goals

Less friction, more done

Centralize AI in one unified experience that drives adoption.

Constraints

Security, compliance, ServiceNow

A healthcare environment with strict governance, rolled out in phases.

What we heard

Four findings that reshaped the brief.

01

Too many tools, too much switching

People jump between separate apps for search, documents, tickets, and tasks. Every hop adds friction and slows the real work down.

02

Fast answers beat fancy AI

Users ranked quick answers, document uploads, and ticket creation far above advanced capabilities. Speed to information was the real prize.

03

Document upload isn't optional

PDFs, Word, Excel, and reports are daily reality. Upload and analysis is essential to fit how people actually work.

04

Security and governance, from day one

Stakeholders were firm: secure access, approved models, auditability, and compliance can't be a later phase.

The decision

So we drew a line.

The findings pointed to a small set of high-value, low-effort capabilities. Everything else could wait for evidence.

Value vs effort, how the call was madeMVP, build now Deferred

How the options compared

Safe was the baseline. Useful was the point.

The old tool was safe but weak. ChatGPT was capable but couldn't touch our systems, and wasn't safe for our data. Inova Assist had to be all three: capable, able to act in our tools, and safe by where it ran.

My role

I owned it end to end.

I ran the research, decided what to build, made the design system, and designed every screen and flow, the chat, the file work, the ticketing, and the meetings. Six weeks, no extra time.

With no dedicated PM, I also owned the product. The hard part wasn't the screens. It was getting people to leave a tool they already liked, by making this one do more of their actual work.

What I owned, the calls

Phase one did the work. Phase two scales it.

A safe chat alone wouldn't move anyone, so phase one had to ship the actions that gave people a reason to switch. I scored features by impact against effort and drew the line between the two phases.

Phase 1, shipped, the reason to switch
1Chat plus saved history
2Ask about an uploaded file
3Create and manage ServiceNow tickets
4Summarize and set up meetings
5Fast / Thinking model choice
6One-time safety agreement
7Report a problem, settings, dark mode
Phase 2, next, scale into their tools
→Copilot across Word, Excel, SharePointBring the assistant into the Office apps staff live in, so the work comes to them.
→Deeper ticket and workflow automationMore of the routine IT and ops actions handled end to end from chat.
→Power BI developer integrationsHook into Power BI so analysts and developers can query datasets and pull reports straight from the assistant.
Why Copilot is next, not first: high impact, but a lighter lift than it looks, because it rides the Copilot layer Microsoft already ships inside those apps. Phase one earned the right to scale by proving the actions people actually wanted.

Key decisions

Three decisions that mattered most.

Standing up a safe model is infrastructure, and engineering owned it. Getting staff to leave a tool they liked is the design problem. These three did that.

01

Make it act in their tools, not just answer

The top requests were actions: open a ticket, summarize a meeting, read a file. So I designed the assistant to take those actions inside their systems, with a clear confirmation and a visible result, instead of stopping at advice. That is the reason to switch a developer's chat wrapper would have missed.

A real reason to leave ChatGPT
02

Show what the AI can't do, before people rely on it

A new chat opens with three plain columns: what it's good at, what it remembers, and where it gets things wrong. In a hospital, someone acting on a confident wrong answer is the real danger, so I set expectations before the first question, not after a bad one.

Trust, calibrated
03

Make the meeting summary a conversation, not a file

Most summary tools dump a document and stop. I dropped the summary back into the chat as a message you can question, so people pull the to-dos, check a decision, or draft the follow-up without leaving. That's the difference between a feature and a reason to come back.

A reason to stay

Layout locked in rough sketches first.

I worked out the sidebar, chat area, model choice, safety screen, file upload, and the action flows as simple sketches before any visuals. It kept the conversations with IT and compliance grounded in something real to point at.

A closer look

Raising a ticket, without leaving the chat.

One of the actions people asked for most. Describe the issue in plain words, the assistant drafts the Service Hub ticket, and you confirm, so it's filed without ever leaving the chat.

1

Describe the issue

Say what's wrong; it asks only what it still needs.

2

Review the draft

Every field pre-filled, ready to check before it sends.

3

Submit and done

One tap files it and the ticket ID lands in the chat.

Step 1 · Describe the issue

Start from a sentence

No ticket form to learn. A plain request is enough, and it fills the gaps with a few short questions.

Step 2 · Review the draft

Check, don't retype

Request type, category, urgency, all pre-filled from the chat. Edit anything, or submit as is.

Step 3, the ticket is filed in Service Hub and the ID comes straight back into the chat, ready to track.

Why this choice matters. A draft you confirm beats a form you fill. Pre-filling every field from the conversation turned a multi-screen portal task into a glance and a tap.

A closer look

Summing up a meeting, in three steps.

One of the actions people asked for most. Three steps, and the summary lands right in the chat, so you can question it, not just read it.

1

Pick a date

Choose the day the meeting happened.

2

Pick a meeting

Choose from that day's list.

3

Get the summary

It appears in the chat, ready to question.

Step 1 · Pick a date

Choose the day

One choice per screen. The calendar opens on a set date, so no one starts from a blank box.

Step 2 · Pick a meeting

Choose from that day

Each meeting shows how long it ran, so a quick sync reads differently from a long one. Pick one, then create the summary.

Step 3, the summary lands in the chat: subject, who was there, an overview, and the full notes, as a message you can reply to.

Why this choice matters. Most summary tools dump a file and stop. By dropping the summary back into the chat, people keep going, pull the to-dos, draft the follow-up, without leaving. That's what makes an action feel like part of the work, not a detour.

Results from testing

Two numbers, both from real users.

I tested with two groups of 8, clinical staff, operations, and IT. These two numbers are the ones worth talking about.

91%
finished their task, up from 68% in round one
What I changed between rounds
  • People got stuck on the agreement screen, "Cancel" looked like "quit." I changed the buttons to "Accept" and "Decline." Drop-off went to zero
  • People ignored the model numbers. Adding the words "Fast" and "Thinking" fixed it right away
  • Upload and the action buttons were hard to find. Moving them solved it in one round
8 / 8
said they'd use it instead of their old workaround
How I asked
  • I asked: would you use this, or find another way? In round two, all 8 said yes, up from 5
  • The reason they gave most was that it did things ChatGPT couldn't, tickets and meeting summaries in one place
  • This is the number that counts. The tool only wins if it replaces the workaround, not just if people can finish a task in a test

Why people switched

Adoption was a design problem.

It did things ChatGPT couldn't

I designed the action flows, raising and managing ServiceNow tickets, working on files, summarizing meetings, so the assistant saved real steps instead of just answering. That was the reason to switch.

It dropped people straight in

Designed the entry to open already signed in through hospital SSO, no account, no login wall. Starting it cost nothing, so trying it beat reaching for ChatGPT on a phone.

It never felt like a downgrade

Capability on the first screen and the model choice in plain words, so people could see it matched ChatGPT and lost nothing by moving.

It felt allowed, not policed

Designed to read as sanctioned and calm, plain language, no alarming compliance UI, so people did real work without the gray-area guilt.

The safety came from where this runs, an OpenAI model inside the hospital's own governed environment. That was the constraint, not the contribution. The design and product job was everything that got people to choose it over the ChatGPT on their phone, making it do their actual work, keeping it as capable, and getting out of the way.
What I'd do differently

Wire up the integrations sooner.

The actions were what made people switch, so the connections to ServiceNow and files were the highest-leverage work. If I ran it again, I'd start that plumbing alongside the design from day one, instead of racing it near the end.

The bigger lesson

A safe tool no one uses protects no one.

IT can stand up a compliant model in a tenant. That doesn't move a single person off the workaround they already trust. The design work, and the only thing that actually lowers risk, was making the sanctioned tool genuinely more useful. Adoption was the real safety.
